title: Model Artifact Integrity
summary: This intermediate module teaches you to verify that a model artifact matches an approved artifact, assess its documented origin and intended use, and distinguish byte-level integrity from source authentication. After completing it, you can apply a repeatable acceptance check before using or distributing an artifact.
objectives: Compare an artifact's computed digest with a trusted expected digest.
Explain why a matching digest does not by itself authenticate an artifact's source.
Review model and dataset documentation for origin, intended use, evaluation, and relevant limitations.
Decide whether to accept, reject, or isolate an artifact when integrity evidence is incomplete.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous citation, content/modules/self-hosted-model-operations/model-artifact-integrity.json, had an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. Whether that source moved is UNKNOWN. It passed the review requirement because no successful verification was recorded.

That citation was removed and replaced with resolvable primary sources covering cryptographic hashes, digital signatures, model reporting, and dataset documentation. The correction affects the module's source traceability and the support for its integrity-checking guidance.

sections.title: What artifact integrity means
paragraphs: In this module, a model artifact is the file or set of files delivered for storage, evaluation, deployment, or redistribution. Integrity checking asks whether the received bytes match the bytes approved by the organization or person accepting the artifact.

A cryptographic hash function produces a fixed-length digest from input data. Recomputing the digest for a received artifact and comparing it with a trusted expected digest can reveal whether the received bytes differ from the approved bytes. The comparison must be exact.

A matching digest is evidence of equality with the bytes represented by the expected digest. It is not, by itself, evidence about who created or approved those bytes. If an untrusted party can replace both an artifact and its recorded digest, the comparison does not establish a trustworthy origin.
sections.callout: Treat the expected digest as security-relevant evidence. Obtain it through an approved channel rather than from the same untrusted location as the artifact.

sections.title: Check origin separately
paragraphs: Origin authentication is a separate question from byte comparison. Digital signatures can provide evidence that signed data came from the holder of a signing key and was not modified after signing, provided the verifier already has a trustworthy basis for associating the verification key with the claimed signer.

Record where the artifact came from, who approved it, when it was received, and which expected digest or signature was used. If the artifact's claimed origin cannot be connected to trusted evidence, its origin is UNKNOWN and the artifact should not be treated as authenticated.
Do not infer authenticity merely because a file name, directory, download page, or accompanying text looks familiar. Those labels are not substitutes for trusted integrity and origin evidence.

sections.title: Review the accompanying documentation
paragraphs: Artifact review also needs documentation about appropriate use. Model Cards for Model Reporting describes documentation that includes intended use, evaluation information, and limitations. A digest can show that documentation has not changed relative to an expected copy, but it cannot show that the documented model is suitable for a particular use.

Datasheets for Datasets proposes documenting a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and other characteristics. When dataset information is relevant to evaluating a model artifact, confirm that the available documentation identifies the applicable data and describes limitations that affect the planned use.

Missing documentation does not prove that the artifact's bytes were altered. It does mean that suitability, provenance, or limitations may remain UNKNOWN. Keep that uncertainty separate from the result of the byte-level integrity check.

sections.title: Apply a repeatable acceptance procedure
paragraphs: First, identify the exact artifact being reviewed and the trusted record that describes the approved artifact. Record the claimed origin, approval context, and expected digest or signature evidence before relying on the artifact.

Second, compute a digest over the received artifact and compare it exactly with the trusted expected digest. A mismatch means the received bytes are not the approved bytes represented by that digest. Stop the acceptance process and isolate the artifact for investigation.

Third, verify origin evidence separately when authentication is required. Then review the accompanying model and dataset documentation for intended use, evaluation, provenance, and relevant limitations.

Accept the artifact only when the evidence required by the receiving organization's process is present and consistent. Reject or isolate it when a digest mismatches, origin evidence fails, records conflict, or required information remains UNKNOWN. Record the decision and the evidence used so that another reviewer can repeat the check.

sections.title: Intermediate-level scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand files, downloads, and the basic idea of approving an artifact for later use. It does not assume prior cryptography expertise.

The module teaches how to interpret digest and signature evidence, not how to design cryptographic algorithms or build a signing system. Those advanced tasks require additional security engineering knowledge and an organization-specific trust model.

questions.prompt: What does an exact match between a computed artifact digest and a trusted expected digest establish?
choices: The received bytes match the bytes represented by the expected digest.
The artifact is suitable for every intended use.
The artifact was created by the person named in its file name.
questions.explanation: A matching digest supports byte-level integrity relative to the trusted expected digest. It does not independently establish origin, suitability, or documentation completeness.

questions.prompt: Why is a digest downloaded from the same untrusted location as an artifact insufficient for authenticating the artifact's origin?
choices: A digest can be used only for text files.
An untrusted party could replace both the artifact and the recorded digest.
Every digest changes each time it is read.
A digest always identifies the artifact's author.
questions.explanation: If the same untrusted party controls both values, it can provide a replacement artifact and a matching replacement digest. The comparison therefore lacks independent origin evidence.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer conclude when required suitability documentation is missing but the artifact digest matches?
choices: The matching digest proves that the artifact is suitable.
The artifact must have been altered.
Byte-level integrity may pass, while suitability or provenance remains UNKNOWN.
Documentation is unnecessary whenever a digest matches.
questions.explanation: Integrity and suitability are separate questions. A digest match can support byte equality, while missing documentation leaves other required conclusions UNKNOWN.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate immediate response when the computed digest does not match the trusted expected digest?
choices: Accept the artifact if its file name is familiar.
Change the expected digest to match the received artifact.
Ignore the mismatch if documentation is present.
Stop acceptance and isolate the artifact for investigation.
questions.explanation: A mismatch means the received bytes are not the approved bytes represented by the expected digest. Acceptance should stop until the discrepancy is investigated.
